chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Ibrahim ibn Hashim from Amr ibn Uthman from Muhammad ibn Udhafir from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

In Kufa there are cursed mosques and blessed mosques. As for the blessed one, it is the Mosque of Ghani, and by God, its qibla is slanted and its clay is good, and a believing man laid it down, and the world will not pass away until two springs burst forth for it, and two gardens will be under it, and its people are cursed and it is taken away from them. And the Mosque of Bani Dhafar, which is the Mosque of Al-Sahla, and the Mosque of Al-Hamra, and the Mosque of Ju'fi, and it is not their mosque today.

And as for the cursed mosques, they are the Mosque of Thaqif, and the Mosque of Al-Ash'ath, and the Mosque of Jarir ibn Abdillah Al-Bajali, and the Mosque of Simak, and the Mosque of Al-Hamra, which was built on the grave of Pharaoh from the Pharaohs.

key_terms.بُنِيَ عَلَى قَبْرِ فِرْعَوْنَ: Built on the grave of Pharaoh

ai.seo_question: What are the characteristics that distinguish blessed mosques from cursed mosques in Kufa according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between blessed and cursed mosques in Kufa, highlighting that spiritual merit is not always tied to physical grandeur or the piety of the founders. The narration specifically notes that the mosque of Ghani, despite its correct qibla and quality construction, is associated with a cursed lineage, while the mosque of Al-Hamra is built upon the grave of a Pharaoh, linking architectural history to theological status. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the interplay between physical sanctity and the moral/spiritual state of the community or founders.
